chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Abu Ayyub from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

When a man divorces his wife while he is absent from her, he should bear witness regarding that; and when three months have passed, her waiting period (iddah) is completed, and the one whose husband dies while he is absent from her, she observes the waiting period when his death reaches her.

Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn Mahziyar from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Ash'ari who said: Some of our mawlas wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) with me, saying: A known woman, her husband caused a commotion (or went into seclusion) and fled in the land, so some of the woman's people pursued the husband and said: Either you have divorced her or I will return you, so he divorced her and the man went on his way. What do you think regarding the woman? He wrote in his hand: 'Marry, may Allah have mercy on you.'
ai.seo_question: What is the waiting period (iddah) for a woman whose husband is absent or has fled?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Baqir (AS) clarifies the procedural validity of divorce (talaq) when the husband is absent, emphasizing the necessity of witnesses to prevent disputes over the timing of the decree. It establishes a three-month waiting period (iddah) for absent husbands, contrasting with the standard three menstrual cycles, and specifies that the waiting period for a deceased absent husband begins only upon the wife's receipt of news. The second report illustrates the practical application of these rules, where a fleeing husband's confirmed divorce allows the wife immediate remarriage, highlighting the Shia emphasis on legal certainty and the Imam's authoritative interpretation of marital status.
